In mathematics, '''structural Ramsey theory''' is a [[:Category theory|categorical]] generalisation of [[Ramsey theory]], rooted in the idea that many important results of Ramsey theory have "similar" logical structures. The key observation is noting that these Ramsey-type theorems can be expressed as the assertion that a certain category (or class of finite structures) has the '''Ramsey property''' (defined below).

Structural Ramsey theory began in the 1970s<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Nguyen Van Thé|first=Lionel|date=2014-12-10|title=A survey on structural Ramsey theory and topological dynamics with the Kechris–Pestov–Todorcevic correspondence in mind|eprint=1412.3254|class=math.CO}}</ref> with the work of [[Jaroslav Nešetřil|Nešetřil]] and [[Vojtěch Rödl|Rödl]], and is intimately connected to [[Fraïssé limit|Fraïssé theory]]. It received some renewed interest in the mid-2000s due to the discovery of the '''Kechris–Pestov–Todorčević correspondence''', which connected structural Ramsey theory to [[topological dynamics]].

== Motivation ==

This article will use the [[set theory]] convention that each natural number <math>n \in \mathbb{N}</math> can be considered as the set of all natural numbers less than it: i.e. <math>n = \{ 0, 1, \ldots, n-1 \}</math>. For any set <math>A</math>, an ''<math>r</math>-colouring of <math>A</math>'' is an assignment of one of <math>r</math> labels to each element of <math>A</math>. This can be represented as a function <math>\Delta: A \to r</math> mapping each element to its label in <math>r = \{ 0, 1, \ldots, r-1 \}</math> (which this article will use), or equivalently as a partition of <math>A = A_{0} \sqcup \cdots \sqcup A_{r-1}</math> into <math>r</math> pieces.

Here are some of the classic results of Ramsey theory:

* (Finite) [[Ramsey's theorem]]: for every <math>k \leq m, r \in \mathbb{N}</math>, there exists <math>n \in \mathbb{N}</math> such that for every <math>r</math>-colouring <math>\Delta: [n]^{(k)} \to r</math> of all the <math>k</math>-element subsets of <math>n = \{ 0, 1, \ldots, n-1 \}</math>, there exists a subset <math>A \subseteq n</math>, with <math>|A|=m</math>, such that <math>[A]^{(k)}</math> is <math>\Delta</math>-monochromatic.
* (Finite) [[van der Waerden's theorem]]: for every <math>m, r \in \mathbb{N}</math>, there exists <math>n \in \mathbb{N}</math> such that for every <math>r</math>-colouring <math>\Delta: n \to r</math> of <math>n</math>, there exists a <math>\Delta</math>-monochromatic [[arithmetic progression]] <math>\{ a, a+d, a+2d, \ldots, a+(m-1)d \} \subseteq n</math> of length <math>m</math>.
* [[Graham–Rothschild theorem]]: fix a finite alphabet <math>L = \{ a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{d-1} \}</math>. A ''<math>k</math>-[[parametric word|parameter word]] of length <math>n</math> over <math>L</math>'' is an element <math>w \in (L \cup \{ x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_{k-1} \})^n</math>, such that all of the ''<math>x_i</math>'' appear, and their first appearances are in increasing order. The set of all <math>k</math>-parameter words of length <math>n</math> over <math>L</math> is denoted by <math>\textstyle [L]\binom{n}{k}</math>. Given <math>\textstyle w \in [L]\binom{n}{m}</math> and <math>\textstyle v \in [L]\binom{m}{k}</math>, we form their ''composition'' <math>\textstyle w \circ v \in [L]\binom{n}{k}</math> by replacing every occurrence of ''<math>x_i</math>'' in ''<math>w</math>'' with the ''<math>i</math>''th entry of ''<math>v</math>''.<br>Then, the Graham–Rothschild theorem states that for every <math>k \leq m, r \in \mathbb{N}</math>, there exists <math>n \in \mathbb{N}</math> such that for every <math>r</math>-colouring <math>\textstyle \Delta: [L]\binom{n}{k} \to r</math> of all the <math>k</math>-parameter words of length <math>n</math>, there exists <math>\textstyle w \in [L]\binom{n}{m}</math>, such that <math>\textstyle w \circ [L]\binom{m}{k} = \{ w \circ v: v \in [L]\binom{m}{k} \}</math> (i.e. all the <math>k</math>-parameter subwords of <math>w</math>) is <math>\Delta</math>-monochromatic.
*(Finite) [[Folkman's theorem]]: for every <math>m, r \in \mathbb{N}</math>, there exists <math>n \in \mathbb{N}</math> such that for every <math>r</math>-colouring <math>\Delta: n \to r</math> of <math>n</math>, there exists a subset <math>A \subseteq n</math>, with <math>|A|=m</math>, such that <math>\textstyle \big( \sum_{k \in A} k \big) < n</math>, and <math>\textstyle \operatorname{FS}(A) = \{ \sum_{k \in B} k : B \in \mathcal{P}(A) \setminus \varnothing \}</math> is <math>\Delta</math>-monochromatic.

These "Ramsey-type" theorems all have a similar idea: we fix two integers <math>k</math> and <math>m</math>, and a set of colours <math>r</math>. Then, we want to show there is some <math>n</math> large enough, such that for every <math>r</math>-colouring of the "substructures" of size <math>k</math> inside <math>n</math>, we can find a suitable "structure" <math>A</math> inside <math>n</math>, of size <math>m</math>, such that all the "substructures" <math>B</math> of <math>A</math> with size <math>k</math> have the same colour.

What types of structures are allowed depends on the theorem in question, and this turns out to be virtually the only difference between them. This idea of a "Ramsey-type theorem" leads itself to the more precise notion of the Ramsey property (below).

== The Ramsey property ==
Let <math>\mathbf{C}</math> be a [[:Category (mathematics)|category]]. <math>\mathbf{C}</math> has the ''Ramsey property'' if for every natural number <math>r</math>, and all objects <math>A, B</math> in <math>\mathbf{C}</math>, there exists another object <math>D</math> in <math>\mathbf{C}</math>, such that for every <math>r</math>-colouring <math>\Delta: \operatorname{Hom}(A,D) \to r</math>, there exists a [[morphism]] <math>f: B \to D</math> which is <math>\Delta</math>-monochromatic, i.e. the set

::<math>f \circ \operatorname{Hom}(A,B) = \big\{ f \circ g: g \in \operatorname{Hom}(A,B) \big\}</math>

is <math>\Delta</math>-monochromatic.<ref name="DM"/>

Often, <math>\mathbf{C}</math> is taken to be a class of finite <math>\mathcal{L}</math>-structures over some fixed [[Formal language|language]] <math>\mathcal{L}</math>, with [[embedding]]s as morphisms. In this case, instead of colouring morphisms, one can think of colouring "copies" of <math>A</math> in <math>D</math>, and then finding a copy of <math>B</math> in <math>D</math>, such that all copies of <math>A</math> in this copy of <math>B</math> are monochromatic. This may lend itself more intuitively to the earlier idea of a "Ramsey-type theorem".

There is also a notion of a dual Ramsey property; <math>\mathbf{C}</math> has the dual Ramsey property if its [[Dual (category theory)|dual category]] <math>\mathbf{C}^\mathrm{op}</math> has the Ramsey property as above. More concretely, <math>\mathbf{C}</math> has the ''dual Ramsey property'' if for every natural number <math>r</math>, and all objects <math>A, B</math> in <math>\mathbf{C}</math>, there exists another object <math>D</math> in <math>\mathbf{C}</math>, such that for every <math>r</math>-colouring <math>\Delta: \operatorname{Hom}(D,A) \to r</math>, there exists a [[morphism]] <math>f: D \to B</math> for which <math>\operatorname{Hom}(B,A) \circ f</math> is <math>\Delta</math>-monochromatic.

== Examples ==

* Ramsey's theorem: the class of all finite [[Total order#Chains|chains]], with order-preserving maps as morphisms, has the Ramsey property.
* van der Waerden's theorem: in the category whose objects are [[Natural number|finite ordinals]], and whose morphisms are [[Affine transformation|affine maps]] <math>x \mapsto a + dx</math> for <math>a,d \in \mathbb{N}</math>, <math>d \neq 0</math>, the Ramsey property holds for <math>A=1</math>.
*[[Hales–Jewett theorem]]: let ''<math>L</math>'' be a finite alphabet, and for each <math>k \in \mathbb{N}</math>, let <math>X_k = \{ x_0, \ldots, x_{k-1} \}</math> be a set of <math>k</math> variables. Let <math>\mathbf{GR}</math> be the category whose objects are <math>A_k = L \cup X_k</math> for each <math>k \in \mathbb{N}</math>, and whose morphisms <math>A_n \to A_k</math>, for <math>n \geq k</math>, are functions <math>f: X_n \to A_k</math> which are [[Rigidity (mathematics)#Combinatorial use|rigid]] and [[Surjective function|surjective]] on <math>X_k \subseteq A_k = \operatorname{codom}f</math>. Then, <math>\mathbf{GR}</math> has the dual Ramsey property for <math>A = A_0</math> (and <math>B = A_1</math>, depending on the formulation).
*Graham–Rothschild theorem: the category <math>\mathbf{GR}</math> defined above has the dual Ramsey property.

== The Kechris–Pestov–Todorčević correspondence ==
In 2005, [[Alexander S. Kechris|Kechris]], Pestov and [[Stevo Todorčević|Todorčević]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kechris |first1=A. S. |author-link1=Alexander S. Kechris |last2=Pestov |first2=V. G. |last3=Todorcevic |first3=S. |author-link3=Stevo Todorčević |date=February 2005 |title=Fraïssé Limits, Ramsey Theory, and topological dynamics of automorphism groups |journal=Geometric and Functional Analysis |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=106–189 |doi=10.1007/s00039-005-0503-1 |s2cid=6937893 |issn=1016-443X |url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/38566/7/0305241.pdf}}</ref> discovered the following correspondence (hereafter called the '''KPT correspondence''') between structural Ramsey theory, Fraïssé theory, and ideas from topological dynamics.

Let <math>G</math> be a [[topological group]]. For a [[topological space]] <math>X</math>, a ''<math>G</math>-flow'' (denoted <math>G \curvearrowright X</math>) is a [[Continuous group action|continuous action]] of <math>G</math> on <math>X</math>. We say that <math>G</math> is ''extremely amenable'' if any <math>G</math>-flow <math>G \curvearrowright X</math> on a compact space <math>X</math> admits a [[Fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]] <math>x \in X</math>, i.e. the [[Group action (mathematics)|stabiliser]] of <math>x</math> is <math>G</math> itself.

For a [[Fraïssé's theorem|Fraïssé structure]] <math>\mathbf{F}</math>, its [[automorphism]] group <math>\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbf{F})</math> can be considered a topological group, given the topology of [[pointwise convergence]], or equivalently, the [[subspace topology]] induced on <math>\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbf{F})</math> by the space <math>\mathbf{F}^\mathbf{F} = \{ f: \mathbf{F} \to \mathbf{F} \}</math> with the [[product topology]]. The following theorem illustrates the KPT correspondence:<blockquote>'''Theorem (KPT).''' For a Fraïssé structure <math>\mathbf{F}</math>, the following are equivalent:

# The group <math>\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbf{F})</math> of automorphisms of <math>\mathbf{F}</math> is extremely amenable.
# The class <math>\operatorname{Age}(\mathbf{F})</math> has the Ramsey property.
</blockquote>
